extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of literature
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted standards and aesthetic principles drawn from Vladimir Nabokov's biography and writings, useful for writers, translators, and critics aiming for Nabokov-like literary practice (style, structure, translation, and teaching).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid didacticism; aim for higher aesthetic enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: Nabokov believed that novels should not aim to teach and that readers should not merely empathize with characters but that a 'higher' aesthetic enjoyment should be attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize style and structural craft over moralizing or explicit instruction. The point is aesthetic experience: prioritize artistic form and the pleasures of reading rather than delivering lessons or ideologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject 'general ideas' in favor of particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'detested what he saw as "general ideas" in novels' and objected to broad, explanatory contexts displacing close attention to the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on concrete particulars (e.g., spatial specifics, tiny details) rather than abstract thematic exposition. Example: when teaching Ulysses he would insist that students track exactly where characters were in Dublin (with a map) instead of dwelling on complex historical background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe details rather than summarize narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Nabokov wanted his students to describe the details of the novels rather than a narrative of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In criticism and close reading, foreground description of language, imagery, structure, and micro-level features instead of plot summary or paraphrase. This supports aesthetic appreciation and analytic precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actualism over realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Nabokov preferred 'actualism' (attention to actual details) as a guiding aesthetic principle rather than realism understood as mere mimetic representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize verifiable, sensorial particulars and exactness in depiction ('actualism') rather than relying on broad claims to 'realism' or generalized verisimilitude. This influences voice, detail selection, and narrative emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saturate trivial objects with life via precise sensory detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics note Nabokov's ability to 'saturate trivial things with life, sense and psychology'—he noticed colorations, nuances, smells and sounds so that objects acquire unexpected meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fine-grained sensory description to animate ordinary objects and scenes; give inanimate things psychological and symbolic resonance through careful, particularized language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic playfulness: wordplay, anagrams, coinages
rubrics_metrics.description: Nabokov is noted for clever word play, anagrams (e.g., 'Vivian Darkbloom'), solecisms, and verbal inventiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ playful linguistic devices—puns, anagrams, neologisms, surprising syntactic or lexical choices—to enrich texture and produce stylistic effects. Balance play with precision to avoid mere gimmickry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formal puzzles and structural devices
rubrics_metrics.description: His short story 'The Vane Sisters' is famous for an acrostic final paragraph; 'Signs and Symbols' features a character with 'Referential Mania'—Nabokov embeds formal tricks and codes in his fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate structural games (acrostics, hidden messages, metafictional layers, coded endings) as meaningful parts of narrative architecture. Ensure puzzles serve aesthetic or thematic ends rather than empty complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex plots and daring metaphors; versatility of tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Nabokov's fiction is characterized by complex plots, daring metaphors, and a prose style capable of both parody and intense lyricism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for layered plotting and metaphoric inventiveness; cultivate a prose voice that can shift between ironic/parodic register and intense lyricism as demanded by the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modular composition using index cards
rubrics_metrics.description: Nabokov's creative process involved writing sections of text on hundreds of index cards, which he expanded into paragraphs and chapters and rearranged to form the structure of his novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a modular, card-based or block-by-block approach to compose and reorganize material: draft discrete scenes/paragraphs on movable units, then iterate by rearrangement to discover structural shape. This supports non-linear composition and recombination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-translate sensitive passages and embedded poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Nabokov translated many of his own early works into English and 'always translated the poems embedded in his novels and short stories himself' to guard against mistranslation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For translations of one’s own work or of material central to voice/density (especially poetry embedded in prose), prefer self-translation or direct oversight to preserve nuances and avoid degradation by a 'harmful drudge.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Take prosody and formal technique seriously in verse work
rubrics_metrics.description: Nabokov's commentary on Eugene Onegin includes an appendix 'Notes on Prosody' in which he invented terminology and discussed English verse forms before tackling translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend rigorously to metric and prosodic detail when translating or composing verse; be willing to develop or explain technical terms and methods to preserve formal features across languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value originality, invention, concision, harmony and complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Nabokov compared composing chess problems to art: originality, invention, conciseness, harmony, complexity, and 'splendid insincerity' are qualities he admired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for inventive solutions and formal economy; balance complexity with concision and aesthetic harmony. The ideal work is inventive yet disciplined—pleasingly artful rather than merely candid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject poshlost (kitsch) and ideological constraint; favor individualism
rubrics_metrics.description: Nabokov was a proponent of individualism and disdained 'poshlost' (banal kitsch); he rejected ideologies that curtailed individual freedom and expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid kitschy sentimentality, moralistic gestures, and ideological didacticism in favor of distinctive individual voice and artistic autonomy. Use irony or critique to undermine poshlost rather than capitulate to it.
